notation.meaning: Restaurant employment or earnings in location $i$ of pair $p$ in quarter $t$

blocks.md:
1. **Generalizing Card–Krueger.** Every contiguous county pair straddling a state border with a minimum-wage difference, 1990–2006, becomes its own case study.
2. **Earnings rise, employment does not fall.** Earnings elasticity ≈ 0.2 in every specification; employment elasticity ≈ 0 once local controls are used (0.016 in the border-pair sample).
3. **National estimates are biased.** With common time effects the employment elasticity is −0.21: minimum-wage states grew more slowly for unrelated reasons (no Southern state had its own minimum, and the South grew fast).
Why do case studies find small or no job losses while national panels find negative effects, and which identifying assumption is more credible?

[Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW)](note:quarterly-census-of-employment-and-wages-qcew) county-level restaurant employment and earnings (full-service and limited-service), 1990Q1–2006Q2. In 2006 restaurants employed 29.9% of workers paid within 10% of the minimum. 1,139 border counties form 504 pairs with full data; 288 pairs had a minimum-wage differential at some point.

Dynamic (leads and lags) estimates show no pre-trends with local controls and no employment decline after increases.

- Neighboring counties may not share a labor market; cross-border spillovers bias toward zero.
- Pair-by-period effects discard much variation and reduce precision.
- Only one low-wage industry is studied in detail.

sections.heading: In Econ 424 L8 Minimum Wages and Employment

blocks.md: The bridge from a single case study to a national design: it shows how the control group (all states versus neighbors) flips the employment answer, setting up Jha, Neumark and Rodriguez-Lopez's challenge.
